 - $78
Let $f(n,m)$ be minimal such that in $(m,m+f(n,m))$ there exist distinct integers $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ such that $k\mid a_k$ for all $1\leq k\leq n$. Prove that\[\max_m f(n,m) \leq n^{1+o(1)}\]and that\[\max_m (f(n,m)-f(n,n))\to \infty.\]
#711: [ErPo80][Er92c,p.36]
number theory
A problem of Erdős and Pomerance [ErPo80], who proved that\[\max_m f(n,m) \ll n^{3/2}\]and\[n\left(\frac{\log n}{\log\log n}\right)^{1/2} \ll f(n,n)\ll n(\log n)^{1/2}.\]In [Er92c] Erdős offered 1000 rupees for a proof of either; for uniform comparison across prizes I have converted this using the 1992 exchange rates.
van Doorn [vD26] has provided an affirmative answer to the second question, proving that, for all large $n$, there exists $m=m(n)$ such that\[f(n,m)-f(n,n) \gg \frac{\log n}{\log\log n}n.\]See also [710].
Additional thanks to: Zach Hunter and Wouter van Doorn

 Perhaps especially appropriate to share on 7/11, I've written a short note that I think(?) strengthens the lower-bound scale in the second part of 711. (Currently hosted on my personal site here; will share arXiv link when I have it.)
Writing \(F(n):=\max_m f(n,m)\), the main result is\[
 \liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac{F(n)-f(n,n)}{n\log n}\ge \frac{1}{e}.
\]Since \(f(n,n)=o(n\log n)\), this corresponds to \(F(n)\ge (1/e-o(1))\,n\log n\), strengthening van Doorn's bound.
The proof adapts the Erdős–Pomerance smooth-number obstruction away from the diagonal, using starting points \(m\asymp n\log n\) and smoothness threshold \(y\asymp\log n\). The needed local control for \(\Psi(x,y)\) comes from the saddle-point estimates of Hildebrand–Tenenbaum. The \(n\log n\) scale appears intrinsic to the method, so the result is consistent with the conjectured upper bound in the first question.
As detailed in the paper's acknowledgments, this work was LLM-assisted, and in particular GPT-5.6 Sol made a crucial observation, as did Refine.ink. The final writeup and any errors are my own.
Comments and/or corrections are very welcome!

 Scott already knows this, but for people wanting a short explanation of the proof of the lower bound $\max_m f(n, m) \gg n \log n$; 
Let $\Psi(x, y)$ be the number of $y$-smooth integers in $[1, x]$. Lemma $1$ in [ErPo80] then states the following:
Lemma 1.
If $y, N$ are such that $\frac{n + N}{y} < n$ and $$\Psi(n, y) - \Psi\left(\frac{n+N}{y},y\right) > \Psi(n+N,y) - \Psi(n,y),$$then $f(n, n) > N$.
Noah Lebowitz-Lockard and GPT independently observed that the following straight-forward generalization also holds:
Lemma 2.
If $y, N$ are such that $\frac{m + N}{y} < n$ and $$\Psi(n, y) - \Psi\left(\frac{m+N}{y},y\right) > \Psi(m+N,y) - \Psi(m,y),$$then $f(n, m) > N$.
Noah explained to me that he had intention of using this generalization in order to prove lower bounds on $f(n, m)$, but I don't think he had fully worked it out yet. In any case, the idea GPT came up with is to use the following result of Hildebrand-Tenenbaum (see e.g. Corollary 1.7 here, and note that I'm being a bit unsafe with error terms, but I hope it doesn't invalidate the conclusion):
Lemma 3.
For all $1 \le c \le y \le x$ we have $$\Psi(cx, y) = \Psi(x, y)c^{(1 + o(1))\frac{\log(1 + y/\log x)}{\log y}}.$$We need to apply Lemma 3 three times; with $y = 2 \log n$, we choose $$(c, x) = (4, \textstyle{\frac{1}{4}}n), \qquad (c, x) = (\textstyle{\frac{3}{2}}, \textstyle{\frac{1}{3}}n \log n), \qquad \text{and} \qquad (c, x) = (\frac{1}{3}\log n, n).$$Ignoring $1 + o(1)$ error terms even further, this gives:
\begin{align*}
\Psi(n, y) &= \Psi(\textstyle{\frac{1}{4}}n, y)4^{\frac{\log 3}{\log \log n}} = \Psi(\textstyle{\frac{1}{4}}n, y) \left(1 - \frac{\log 3 \log 4}{\log \log n} \right)^{-1}, \\
\Psi(\textstyle{\frac{1}{2}}n \log n, y) &= \Psi(\textstyle{\frac{1}{3}}n \log n, y) (3/2)^{\frac{\log 3}{\log \log n}} = \Psi(\textstyle{\frac{1}{3}}n \log n, y)\left(1 + \frac{\log 3 \log(3/2)}{\log \log n} \right), \\
\Psi(\textstyle{\frac{1}{3}}n \log n, y) &= 3\Psi(n, y).
\end{align*}Now we choose $m = \frac{1}{3}n \log n$ and $N = \frac{1}{6}n \log n$. Then the left-hand side of Lemma 2 becomes $$\Psi(n, y) - \Psi\left(\frac{m+N}{y},y\right) = \Psi(n, y) - \Psi\left(\textstyle{\frac{1}{4}}n,y\right) = \left(\frac{\log 3 \log 4}{\log \log n}\right)\Psi(n, y),$$ while the right-hand side becomes $$\Psi(m+N,y) - \Psi(m,y) = \left(\frac{3 \log 3 \log(3/2)}{\log \log n}\right)\Psi(n, y).$$Since $\log 4 > 3 \log(3/2)$, the required inequality of Lemma 2 does indeed hold, so we may conclude $$f(n, m) > N \gg n \log n.$$It is noteworthy that, if we knew $$f(n, n) \gg n \sqrt{\log n},$$then the proof (which uses $m \asymp \frac{n \log n}{\log \log n}$) of $$f(n, m) \gg \frac{n \log n}{\log \log n}$$would, with applying $m \asymp n \log n$ instead, actually show $$f(n, m) \gg n \log n$$as well.

 Remarkably, it seems that this problem (morally, at least) implies the Kakeya conjecture in all dimensions! Proof sketch: if the Kakeya conjecture failed, then by the tensor power trick we conclude that for sufficiently high dimension $d$, there exists Kakeya sets of dimension less than $d-1$. Discretizing (and taking some liberties with the analogy between arithmetic progressions and tubes), we get about $N^{d-1}$ arithmetic progressions of spacing $\sim N$ that occupy less than $N^{d-1}$ elements, so it is not possible to assign each such progression a distinct element. Morally, one can then invoke the Chinese remainder theorem to conclude.

 It corresponds to 3D Kakeya sets having dimension at least 2, which can be established by elementary incidence geometry (mostly using the fact that two lines intersect in at most one point).
This suggests that the sums-differences approach of Bourgain (I also worked on this with Nets Katz) to Kakeya in high dimensions may make progress on this 3/2 exponent. This article of Green and Ruzsa may be a starting point for anyone wanting to pursue this. (Incidentally, Conjecture 5 from that paper relates to a problem of Erdos and Selfridge - is it already on this site?)
